source_text: Καὶ μὴν ζῶντα ἔλαβε, καὶ ὑγιῆ κατήγαγε· πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἐφείσατο; Ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ τοῦ τέλους τῶν πραγμάτων, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς προ θέσεως τῶν προελομένων, τὰς τοιαύτας κρίνω θυσίας ἐγὼ, φησίν. Οὐκ ἔσφαξεν ἡ χεὶρ, ἀλλ' ἔσφαξεν ἡ προαίρεσις· οὐκ ἐβάπτισε τὸ ξίφος εἰς τὸν λαιμὸν τοῦ παιδὸς, οὐ διέτεμε τὴν δέρην, ἀλλ' ἔστι θυσία καὶ χωρὶς αἵματος. Ἴσασιν οἱ μεμυημένοι τὸ λεγόμενον· διὰ τοῦτο δὲ κἀκείνη ἡ θυσία χωρὶς αἵματος ἐγένετο, ἐπειδὴ ταύτης ἔμελλεν ἔσεσθαι τύπος. Ὁρᾷς ἐν τῇ Παλαιᾷ προδιαγραφομένην τὴν εἰκόνα; Μὴ ἀπιστή σῃς τῇ ἀληθείᾳ. γʹ. Οὗτος τοίνυν ὁ μάρτυς (μάρτυρα γὰρ ἡμῖν αὐτὸν ὁ λόγος ἀπέδειξε) πρὸς μυρίους παρεσκευάσατο θανάτους, καὶ πάντας αὐτοὺς ὑπέμεινε τῇ γνώμῃ καὶ τῇ προθυμίᾳ· τῶν δὲ ἐπενεχθέντων κινδύνων πολλοὺς καὶ δι' αὐτῆς τῆς πείρας ἠνέσχετο. Καὶ γὰρ καὶ τῆς πατρίδος αὐτὸν ἐξήλασαν, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ὑπερορίαν μετέστησαν, καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα κατὰ τοῦ μακαρίου ἐκίνησαν τότε ἐκείνου, δίκαιον μὲν οὐδὲν ἔχοντες ἐγκαλεῖν, ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος, Ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα, ἔφυγε τὸ ἀσέβημα, καὶ τὴν παρανομίαν ἔδεισεν· ἀλλὰ τοῦτο μὲν στεφάνων, οὐ κατηγορίας ἄξιον. Σὺ δέ μοι σκόπει τοῦ διαβόλου τὴν πονηρίαν. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ προσφάτως ἦν ὁ Ἑλληνικὸς πόλεμος καταλυθεὶς, καὶ ἄρτι τῶν χαλεπῶν καὶ ἐπαλλήλων διωγμῶν ἀνεπεπνεύκεισαν αἱ Ἐκκλησίαι πᾶσαι, καὶ οὐκ ἦν πολὺς ὁ χρόνος, ἐξ οὗ λαοὶ μὲν ἀπεκλείσθησαν ἅπαντες, βωμοὶ δὲ ἐσβέσθησαν, πᾶσα δὲ τῶν δαι μόνων ἡ μανία καταλέλυτο, καὶ ταῦτα ἐλύπει τὸν πονηρὸν δαίμονα, καὶ οὐκ ἠδύνατο πράως φέρειν τὴν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας εἰρήνην, τί οὖν ποιεῖ; Ἕτερον ἐπεισ-άγει πόλεμον χαλεπόν. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐξωτικὸς, οὗτος δὲ ἐμφύλιος ἦν· οἱ δὲ τοιοῦτοι δυσφύλακτοι μᾶλλόν εἰσι, καὶ ῥᾳδίως χειροῦνται τοὺς ἐμπίπτοντας. Κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοίνυν ἐκεῖνον ὁ μακάριος οὗτος ἐστρατήγει τῆς παρ' ἡμῖν Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ αἴρεται μὲν ἡ νόσος, ὥσπερ τις λοιμὸς χαλεπὸς ἀπὸ τῶν Αἰγύπτου χωρίων, εἶτα διὰ τῶν μεταξὺ πόλεων βαδίζων εἰς τὴν πόλιν ἔσπευδεν ἐμβαλεῖν τὴν ἡμετέραν. Ἀλλ' ἐκεῖνος ἐγρηγορὼς καὶ νήφων, καὶ πάντα τὰ μέλλοντα προορῶν πόῤῥωθεν, προσιόντα τὸν πόλεμον ἀπεκρούετο· καὶ καθάπερ σοφός τις ἰατρὸς, πρὶν ἢ τὴν νόσον ἐμβαλεῖν εἰς τὴν πόλιν, ἐνταῦθα καθήμενος, τὰ φάρμακα κατεσκεύαζε, καὶ τὴν ἱερὰν ταύτην ναῦν μετὰ πολλῆς ἐκυβέρνα τῆς ἀσφαλείας, παντα χοῦ περιτρέχων, ναύτας, ἐπιβάτας, τοὺς πλέοντας ἅπαντας συγκροτῶν, νήφειν, ἐγρηγορέναι παρασκευάζων, ὡς πειρατῶν ἐπιτιθεμένων καὶ τῆς πίστεως τὸν θησαυρὸν ἀποσυλῆσαι ἐπιχειρούντων. Οὐκ ἐνταῦθα δὲ μόνον ἐκέχρητο τῇ προνοίᾳ ταύτῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ παντα χοῦ διεπέμπετο τοὺς διδάξοντας, παρακαλέσοντας, διαλεξομένους, προαποτειχίσοντας τοῖς πολεμίοις τὴν ἔφοδον. Καὶ γὰρ ἦν πεπαιδευμένος καλῶς παρὰ τῆς τοῦ Πνεύματος χάριτος, ὅτι τὸν Ἐκκλησίας προ εστῶτα οὐκ ἐκείνης μόνης κήδεσθαι δεῖ τῆς παρὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος ἐγχειρισθείσης αὐτῷ, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσης τῆς κατὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην κειμένης· καὶ ταῦτα ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερῶν ἐμάνθανεν εὐχῶν. Εἰ γὰρ τὰς εὐχὰς ποιεῖ σθαι δεῖ, φησὶν, ὑπὲρ τῆς καθολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἀπὸ περάτων ἕως περάτων τῆς οἰκουμένης, πολλῷ μᾶλλον καὶ τὴν πρόνοιαν ὑπὲρ ἁπάσης αὐτῆς ἐπι δείκνυσθαι δεῖ, καὶ ὁμοίως ἁπασῶν κήδεσθαι, καὶ μεριμνᾷν πάσας.
thought_title: Intention completes the sacrifice; Eustathius's vigilance against heresy
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining how Abraham's sacrifice was complete without bloodshed, then turns to Eustathius's readiness for death and his defense of the Antiochene church against the Arian heresy.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed he received him living, and brought him down healthy; how then did he not spare him? Because not from the outcome of the deeds, but from the intention of those who chose beforehand, I judge such sacrifices, he says. The hand did not slay, but the intention slew; the sword did not dip into the throat of the child, it did not cut the neck, but it is a sacrifice even without blood. The initiated know what is being said; and for this reason also that sacrifice happened without blood, since it was going to be a type of this one. Do you see in the Old Testament the image being sketched beforehand? Do not disbelieve the truth. 3. This martyr therefore (for the argument has shown him to us as a martyr) prepared himself for ten thousand deaths, and he endured all of them in his resolve and in his readiness; and of the dangers that were brought upon him, he bore many also through actual experience. For indeed they drove him out of his homeland, and they removed him to exile, and they stirred up many other things against that blessed man at that time, having no just charge to bring, but because, having heard Paul saying, They revered and served the creature rather than the creator, he fled the impiety, and he feared the transgression; but this is worthy of crowns, not of accusation. But consider for me the wickedness of the devil. For since the pagan war had recently been brought to an end, and all the churches had just recovered breath from the harsh and successive persecutions, and not much time had passed since all the peoples had been shut out, and the altars had been extinguished, and all the madness of the demons had been dissolved, and these things grieved the evil demon, and he could not bear gently the peace of the church, what then does he do? He introduces another harsh war. For the one was external, but this one was civil; and such wars are harder to guard against, and they easily overpower those who fall into them. At that time therefore this blessed man was commanding the church among us, and the disease arises, like some harsh plague from the regions of Egypt, then walking through the cities between, it was hastening to burst into our city. But that man, wakeful and sober, and foreseeing from afar all the things that were going to happen, was beating back the approaching war; and just as some wise physician, before the disease burst into the city, sitting here, he was preparing the remedies, and he was steering this holy ship with much safety, running around everywhere, encouraging the sailors, the passengers, all those sailing, preparing them to be sober, to be wakeful, since pirates were attacking and attempting to strip away the treasure of the faith. And not only here did he employ this forethought, but he also sent out everywhere those who would teach, who would exhort, who would converse, who would wall off beforehand the attack of the enemies. For indeed he had been well instructed by the grace of the Spirit, that the one who presides over the church must care not only for that church entrusted to him by the Spirit, but also for all the church lying throughout the inhabited world; and these things he learned from the sacred prayers. For if prayers must be made, he says, for the catholic church from the ends to the ends of the inhabited world, much more must the forethought be shown for all of it, and care for all alike, and be anxious for all.

choices.why: The glossary mandates 'intention' for προαίρεσις; πρόθεσις here is a near-synonym in the same semantic field, and 'intention' keeps the argument's terminology consistent.
The glossary requires 'exile' for ὑπερορία, the specific suffering Eustathius endured.
The contrast is between an external war (paganism) and an internal one (heresy); 'civil' captures the sense of war within the household of the church.
The military metaphor continues the war imagery; 'commanding' preserves the sense of a general leading the church.
The compound verb means to build a wall in advance against an attack; the literal rendering preserves the defensive imagery.
The verb is the perfect of ἐγείρω and means to be awake, alert; 'wakeful' preserves the literal sense and the shepherd imagery.

bible_refs.note: Ἐσεβάσθησαν καὶ ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα

pass_b_english: And yet he received him alive and brought him down unharmed. How then did he not spare him? Because, he says, I judge such sacrifices not by the outcome of events but by the intention of those who chose beforehand. The hand did not slaughter, but the intention slaughtered. The sword did not stain the boy's throat, it did not cut his neck—yet it is a sacrifice even without blood. The initiated know what this means. And that sacrifice was made without blood precisely because it was going to be a type of this one. Do you see the image being sketched beforehand in the Old Testament? Do not doubt the reality.

This martyr, then—for our argument has shown him to be a martyr—prepared himself for countless deaths, and he endured them all in his judgment and eagerness. And of the dangers that were brought against him, he bore many through actual experience. For they drove him from his homeland and removed him into exile, and they stirred up many other things against that blessed man at that time, having no just charge to bring, but because he, having heard Paul say, "They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25), he fled the impiety and feared the transgression. But this deserves crowns, not accusation.

Consider with me the wickedness of the devil. Since the war against paganism had recently been brought to an end, and all the churches had just recovered from the harsh and successive persecutions, and not much time had passed since all the peoples had been shut out, the altars extinguished, and every frenzy of the demons destroyed—these things grieved the evil demon, and he could not calmly bear the peace of the church. So what does he do? He introduces another harsh war. The first was external, but this one was civil; and such wars are harder to guard against and easily overpower those who fall into them.

At that time, then, this blessed man was commanding the church among us, and the disease arose like a harsh plague from the regions of Egypt, and then, passing through the cities in between, it hastened to burst into our city. But he was wakeful and sober, and foreseeing all that was coming from afar, he beat back the approaching war. And like a wise physician, before the disease could burst into the city, sitting there he prepared the remedies and piloting this sacred ship with great safety, running everywhere, encouraging the sailors, the passengers, all who were sailing, preparing them to be sober and wakeful, since pirates were attacking and attempting to plunder the treasure of the faith.

Nor did he exercise this care only here, but he also sent out everywhere men who would teach, exhort, discuss, and wall off beforehand the enemy's assault. For he had been well instructed by the grace of the Spirit that the one who presides over a church must care not only for that church entrusted to him by the Spirit, but also for the whole church throughout the world. And this he learned from the sacred prayers. For if prayers must be made, he says, for the catholic church from one end of the world to the other, much more must care be shown for all of it, and one must care for all the churches alike and be anxious for them all.

problems.quote: and not much time had passed since all the peoples had been shut out
problems.why: Source says peoples were 'shut up/included' (ἀπεκλείσθησαν), not 'shut out'; meaning reversed.
problems.fix: all the peoples had been gathered in
problems.ruling: ἀπεκλείσθησαν is passive aorist of ἀποκλείω, meaning 'shut out/excluded', not 'shut up/included'; 'shut out' is correct.

problems.quote: because he had heard Paul say
problems.source_quote: ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος
problems.why: The subject is Eustathius's enemies, not Eustathius: 'because, having heard Paul say...' they accused him. The English makes Eustathius the hearer.
problems.fix: but because, having heard Paul say, 'They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator,' he fled the impiety
problems.ruling: ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας...ἔφυγε: the participial clause's subject is the blessed man who heard Paul and fled, matching English correctly.

edits.old: and not much time had passed since all the peoples had been shut out
edits.new: and not much time had passed since all the peoples had been gathered in

edits.old: but because he had heard Paul say, "They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25), he fled the impiety and feared the transgression.
edits.new: but because, having heard Paul say, "They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25), he fled the impiety and feared the transgression.

fixed: ἀπεκλείσθησαν means 'were shut in/gathered in' (from ἀποκλείω, shut in), not 'shut out'; the English reversed the meaning, so corrected to 'gathered in'.

The source's 'ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος' is a causal clause explaining why the enemies stirred up things against Eustathius: they had heard Paul say... and Eustathius fled the impiety. The English made Eustathius the hearer, so I changed 'because he had heard' to 'because, having heard' to keep the subject ambiguous as in the source, with Eustathius as the one who fled.

problems.quote: Because, God says, I judge such sacrifices
problems.source_quote: τὰς τοιαύτας κρίνω θυσίας ἐγὼ, φησίν
problems.why: φησίν is Chrysostom's own voice, not God's; inserting 'God says' falsely attributes the sentence to God.
problems.fix: Because, he says, I judge such sacrifices not by the outcome of events but by the intention of those who chose.
problems.ruling: φησίν lacks subject; context is Chrysostom's commentary on Abraham/Isaac, not divine speech. 'God says' misattributes speaker.

problems.quote: since all the peoples had been gathered in
problems.why: ἀπεκλείσθησαν means 'were shut out/closed off,' i.e., pagan temples were closed, not 'gathered in.'
problems.fix: since all the peoples had been shut out
problems.ruling: ἀπεκλείσθησαν means 'were shut/closed,' opposite of 'gathered in.' Reverses meaning of source.

edits.old: Because, God says, I judge such sacrifices
edits.new: Because, he says, I judge such sacrifices

edits.old: since all the peoples had been gathered in
edits.new: since all the peoples had been shut out

fixed: Speaker attribution: φησίν is Chrysostom's own voice, not God's; changed 'God says' to 'he says'.
Mistranslation: ἀπεκλείσθησαν means 'were shut out,' not 'gathered in'; restored 'shut out'.

problems.quote: he fled the impiety and feared the transgression
problems.source_quote: ἔφυγε τὸ ἀσέβημα, καὶ τὴν παρανομίαν ἔδεισεν
problems.why: Missing 'but this deserves crowns, not accusation' applies to Eustathius's action, but English makes 'this' ambiguous; more critically, the Greek says Eustathius fled and feared, while enemies had no just charge—English obscures that Eustathius is the subject fleeing heresy
problems.fix: he fled the impiety and feared the transgression; but this deserves crowns, not accusation

problems.quote: having no just charge to bring, but because, having heard Paul say
problems.source_quote: δίκαιον μὲν οὐδὲν ἔχοντες ἐγκαλεῖν, ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας τοῦ Παύλου λέγοντος
problems.why: The 'because' clause is about Eustathius, not his enemies. Enemies had no charge; Eustathius fled impiety because he heard Paul.
problems.fix: having no just charge to bring, but because he, having heard Paul say
problems.ruling: ὅτι δὲ ἀκούσας has nominative ἀκούσας agreeing with subject of ἔφυγε (Eustathius), not enemies; 'because' clause misattributes agency.

problems.quote: he sat here preparing the remedies
problems.why: ἐνταῦθα means 'there/then' in context, not 'here'; he was in Antioch, not present with speaker
problems.fix: sitting there he prepared the remedies
problems.ruling: ἐνταῦθα means 'here' = speaker's location, but subject was in Antioch; 'here' misleads reader about spatial reference

edits.old: having no just charge to bring, but because, having heard Paul say
edits.new: having no just charge to bring, but because he, having heard Paul say

edits.old: he sat here preparing the remedies
edits.new: sitting there he prepared the remedies

fixed: The omission problem is not a real omission; the English already contains 'But this deserves crowns, not accusation.' The ambiguity about 'this' is stylistic, not a mistranslation, so no edit is needed.
The mistranslation is real: the 'because' clause refers to Eustathius, not his enemies. Added 'he' to clarify the subject.
The mistranslation is real: ἐνταῦθα means 'there' in this context, not 'here.' Changed 'he sat here preparing' to 'sitting there he prepared.'

refereed.why: The source quotes Paul but gives no verse reference; adding Romans 1:25 is an editorial addition not in the Greek text.
refereed.fix: They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator
